content: Job satisfaction is defined as personal satisfaction relative to the work situation. It is distinct from the concept of life satisfaction, which is often measured using single-question assessments. Similarly, job satisfaction can also be evaluated using single-item measures. Organizations with higher levels of job satisfaction among their employees tend to achieve greater financial success. One example of a single-item measure is the Dunham Faces scale, which uses images of female faces as Likert scale anchors to assess satisfaction. Physician Job Satisfaction The Society of General Internal Medicine (SGIM) Career Satisfaction Study Group (CSSG) has developed and refined the Physician Worklife Survey through literature reviews and focus groups. This survey is designed to measure physician satisfaction and its contributing factors. The survey includes the following scales: Autonomy Relationships with colleagues Patient care issues (originally labeled as relationships with patients) Relationships with staff Personal time Relationships with patients (originally labeled as intrinsic) Community Pay Administration Resources Other surveys have also been created to assess physician satisfaction, such as the AAFP TransforMED PCMH National Demonstration Project. Factor analysis has been used to identify key elements that contribute to physician well-being. Studies on Physician Satisfaction Several large-scale, multisite studies have been conducted to measure job satisfaction among physicians. These include: ACP-MEMO (Minimizing Error, Maximizing Outcome) AMA-RAND study, 2014 California community clinics and health centers study, 2016 Multi-state Commonwealth PCMH study, 2012
